title: Freeways & Highways
summary: How to enter, drive on and leave a freeway safely, share it with trucks, and handle breakdowns, fatigue, wrong-way drivers, work zones and tolls.

sections.heading: Entering the freeway and ramp meters

blocks.text: The acceleration lane runs beside the main lanes so you can build up to the speed of freeway traffic before you merge. Drivers already on the freeway have the right-of-way, so you must find a safe gap and fit into it.

items: Signal early so freeway drivers know you are coming.
Find a gap using your mirrors and a quick look over your shoulder.
Match your speed to freeway traffic, at or near its speed.
Merge smoothly into the gap.
Avoid stopping in the acceleration lane unless you have no choice. You would then have to enter fast traffic from a standstill, and drivers behind you may not expect it.
If a short entrance has a YIELD sign and no acceleration lane, obey the sign. Stop if needed and wait for a large gap.
If a solid white line separates the entrance lane from the freeway, do not cross it. Merge after the line ends, when there is a safe gap.
When you are already on the freeway and see someone merging, help if you safely can: move left or adjust your speed to make room.

blocks.text: Ramp meters: a ramp meter is a traffic signal on an entrance ramp. It spaces out vehicles entering a busy freeway so they do not all merge at once.

rows: Stop at the stop line and wait.
Go, but you must still yield to freeway traffic when you merge.
Only one vehicle goes on each green. If the car ahead just went, stop and wait for your own green.

items: Pick a lane and stay in it. Weaving from lane to lane raises your crash risk and rarely saves much time.
Rear-end crashes are a leading freeway danger. Keep a safe following distance and look far ahead so you see slowdowns early.
Stop on the freeway or its shoulder only in an emergency or when a police officer tells you to.
HOV and express lanes separated by double solid white lines may be entered or left only at the marked openings.

blocks.text: Freeway speed limits, minimum speeds and HOV rules vary by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Get into the lane you need well before your exit. The heavier the traffic, the earlier you should move over.
If you are several lanes away, change lanes one at a time. Signal and check your blind spot each time.
Keep your speed while on the freeway. Begin slowing once you are in the exit (deceleration) lane.
Most exits are on the right, but some are on the left. Read the signs early and move into the left lane well ahead of a left exit.
If you miss your exit, go on to the next one. Never stop, back up or cross the median.
If you take the wrong exit, continue off the ramp and find your way back. Do not stop or back up on the ramp.

blocks.text: A cloverleaf interchange uses loop-shaped ramps so traffic can get on or off in any direction without crossing in front of other traffic. Loop ramps are tight curves, so slow to the posted ramp speed before the curve.
In a weave lane, entering and exiting traffic share the same short lane. The driver entering the freeway yields to the driver leaving it.

After a long freeway drive, normal street speeds can feel slow, so you may be going faster than you think. When you leave the freeway, check your speedometer and watch for lower limits, two-way traffic, cross streets and pedestrians.

sections.heading: Sharing the highway with large trucks

items: Pass a truck on the left and finish the pass without lingering beside it.
Do not move back in front until you can see the whole front of the truck in your rearview mirror.
If you cannot see the driver's face in the truck's side mirror, the driver probably cannot see you. Speed up or drop back.
On a downgrade a truck's momentum makes it go faster, so a pass takes more speed and time. On an upgrade trucks often lose speed, which makes them easier to pass.
When a truck passes you, keep to the far side of your lane and ease off slightly. Never speed up while it is passing.
Wind blast from a passing truck can push your car sideways. Grip the wheel firmly and keep your lane position.

blocks.text: Highway hypnosis is a drowsy, trance-like state caused by long, dull driving with steady noise and an unchanging view. Prevent it by keeping your eyes moving: look far ahead and to the sides, read signs and check your mirrors.

items: Warning signs of fatigue: you cannot remember the last few miles, you keep yawning, your eyelids feel heavy, you drift out of your lane, miss signs or hit the rumble strip.
When you notice these signs, get off at the next safe place and rest.
On long trips, take a break about every two hours or 100 miles, even if you feel fine.
Coffee, fresh air or the radio may help for a short time, but they do not replace sleep. If you are drowsy, stop.
Do not rely on stay-awake pills or other stimulants. They can make your driving even more dangerous.
If your car starts to fail, signal and steer onto the shoulder, completely out of the travel lanes if you can.
Turn on your hazard (emergency) flashers.
If you must get out, use the door on the side away from traffic and stay away from moving vehicles.
With a flat tire, even in the left lane, do not stop in a travel lane. Slow down gradually and steer off the road.
When you see a disabled vehicle on the shoulder ahead, slow down and give it extra space. Watch for people, tow trucks and police.

blocks.caption: Move Over laws protect people stopped on the shoulder. Details vary by state; check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY signs mark freeway exit ramps. Seeing them facing you means you would be driving against traffic.
If you have just turned onto a ramp the wrong way, back out or turn around when it is safe. This is the one exception to the rule against backing on a ramp.
Pavement reflectors that glow red in your headlights mean you are going the wrong way.
On a divided highway going the right way, the yellow edge line is on your left and the white edge line is on your right.

blocks.text: Wrong-way drivers are often impaired and are usually in the far left lane or the HOV lane. If you see headlights coming straight at you in your lanes, ease off the gas, make sure no one is beside you, and steer away from the oncoming car. Call 911 once you are in a safe place.

items: In a highway work zone, slow down and watch for workers, equipment and shifting lanes. Most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions, so leave extra space.
When you see signs for a toll plaza, slow down early and watch for backed-up traffic and signs showing which lanes take which payment.
If you enter the wrong toll lane, continue through it. Do not back up or cut across.
Leaving a toll booth, watch both sides for merging cars and speed up smoothly.
Electronic toll lanes let drivers with a transponder or toll account pay without stopping.

keyPoints: Use the acceleration lane to reach freeway speed, and yield to traffic already on the freeway.
At a ramp meter, stop on red; a green light lets you go but you must still yield when merging.
Get into your exit lane early, one lane at a time, and slow down only once you are in the exit lane.
Missed your exit? Take the next one. Never stop, back up or cross the median.
Pass trucks on the left, don't linger, and return only when you see the whole truck in your mirror.
If you're drowsy, stop and rest; coffee, fresh air and stay-awake pills don't replace sleep.
If your car fails, get fully onto the shoulder, use your flashers, and exit away from traffic.
DO NOT ENTER, WRONG WAY and red reflectors all mean you're heading against traffic.
